extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners (and patent prosecutors/practitioners advising on §101 issues)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing 35 U.S.C. §101 subject-matter eligibility of claims that recite or involve laws of nature, natural phenomena, or natural products. Shows a three-question framework and factors (a–l) to weigh toward or against whether a claim recites something 'significantly different' than a judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-question eligibility framework (Questions 1-3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stepwise analysis: (1) Is the claim directed to a statutory category (machine, manufacture, composition, or process)? (2) Does the claim recite a judicial exception (law of nature, natural principle, natural phenomenon, natural product, or abstract idea)? (3) Does the claim, as a whole, recite something significantly different than the judicial exception?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If answers to Questions 1–2 are 'yes' (statutory category and judicial exception recited), evaluate Question 3 using the listed factors (a–l). For claims reciting an abstract idea, analyze under MPEP §2106(II) (see separate metric). Examples in the guidance show applying Questions 1–3 to composition, manufacture, process claims and mixed claims (e.g., primers, amplification methods, diagnostic methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor a) Markedly different (product claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: For product claims, whether the claimed natural product(s) are 'markedly different' from what exists in nature (structurally or functionally).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the natural product is not markedly different (e.g., isolated nucleic acids whose sequence and function remain as in nature; naturally occurring bacteria not altered), factor a) is not satisfied and weighs against eligibility. Example: primers whose genetic sequence and function are unchanged are not 'markedly different' (Myriad).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor b) Claim limitations meaningfully narrow scope (avoid substantial foreclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether elements in addition to the judicial exception meaningfully narrow the claim scope so that others are not substantially foreclosed from using the judicial exception in other ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satisfied when specific limits (temperatures/times, particular use/application, choice of synthetic vs natural source, etc.) prevent coverage of substantially all uses of the exception. Example: heating/cooling cycles in an amplification method narrow scope; specifying synthetic white light (vs sunlight) limits scope. If only a field-of-use is claimed (e.g., 'use sunlight to treat mood disorder') and substantially forecloses others, b) is not satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor c) Elements relate to the judicial exception in a significant way
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether claim elements in addition to the judicial exception relate to it in a significant, non-insignificant manner (e.g., physical integration or direct manipulation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satisfied when additional elements materially integrate or manipulate the natural product/principle (e.g., combination forms a structure into which natural products are physically integrated; heating/cooling steps directly manipulate DNA). Examples: cardboard body + ignition fuse integrate calcium chloride and gunpowder physically; thermal cycling directly manipulates DNA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor d) More than mere instructions or description
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether additional claim elements do more than describe the judicial exception or give general instructions to use/apply it (i.e., claim recites a specific practical application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satisfied when the claim as a whole recites a concrete application (e.g., use of a particular antibody and flow cytometry to detect a misfolded protein) rather than a high-level instruction to 'apply' the principle. Unsatisfied when the step is merely 'expose to sunlight' or other general instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor e) Machine-or-transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claim recites a machine or a transformation (the presence of which can weigh toward eligibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no machine or transformation is recited, factor e) is not satisfied. The guidance checks for a recited machine or transformative act as part of eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor f) Additional elements are more than well-understood, purely conventional or routine
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the additional elements contribute something inventive beyond what is well-understood, routine, or conventional in the relevant art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satisfied when the specification/record shows the additional elements are not routine (e.g., a newly created antibody that is not conventional). Unsatisfied when the claimed steps or elements are conventional (e.g., routine heating/cooling in PCR, routine use of antibodies generally).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor g) Natural products are not markedly different (weighs against eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: When natural products recited are not markedly different from their natural counterparts, this factor supports ineligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essentially the 'against eligibility' counterpart to factor a). Example: multiple naturally occurring bacterial strains that are structurally identical to natural bacteria satisfy g) and weigh against eligibility (Funk Brothers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor h) Claim recited at a high level of generality covering substantially all practical applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claimed elements are recited so broadly that the claim covers substantially all practical applications of the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satisfied (weighs against eligibility) when claim language is high-level and covers substantially all applications (e.g., broadly claiming 'expose to white light' without meaningful limits). Not satisfied when specific steps or parameters limit the claim so not all applications are covered (e.g., specified distances/times/filters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor i) Claimed elements required to use the judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claimed elements are required to use or apply the natural products/principle (i.e., everyone using the exception must use the claimed elements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claimed elements are not required (others can practice the exception by other means), i) is not satisfied. Example: use of a particular antibody or Taq polymerase is not required to amplify DNA generally; others may use different enzymes or methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor j) Additional elements are well-understood, purely conventional, and routine (weighs against eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the additional recited elements are themselves conventional and routine, which weighs against eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the extra elements are routine activity in the art (e.g., known PCR thermal cycling steps, routine positioning or exposure steps), j) is satisfied and weighs against eligibility. If an added element is novel/non-conventional (e.g., a newly created antibody), j) is not satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor k) Additional elements are a significant part of the claim (integrated, not merely appended)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether additional elements form an integrated, meaningful part of the claim rather than being merely appended or insignificant extras.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satisfied when additional elements integrate the judicial exception into a practical application (e.g., elements form a structure physically integrating natural products, or steps directly manipulate natural products). Unsatisfied when elements are mere appendages that do not integrate the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor l) Additional elements are substantial limitations, not mere fields of use
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether additional elements impose substantial limitations and do more than attempt to limit the exception to a mere field-of-use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional elements simply restrict use to a field (e.g., 'use sunlight to treat mood disorder' as a field-of-use), l) is satisfied (weighing against eligibility). If the elements represent a specific practical application beyond mere field-of-use, l) is not satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims reciting both an abstract idea and a natural product: apply MPEP §2106(II)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim recites an abstract idea in addition to a natural product or other judicial exception, the analysis should follow the guidance in MPEP §2106(II) for abstract-idea claims, including how a practical application of another exception affects eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance controls whether the claim qualifies as eligible subject matter when an abstract idea is present. Example: a claim whose only step is 'comparing sequences' (an abstract mental process) and recites a wild-type nucleotide sequence should be analyzed under MPEP §2106(II) and was held ineligible in relevant case law (Myriad/AMP).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of revised Form Paragraph ¶7.05.13 for §101 rejections involving laws of nature/natural phenomena/natural products
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting claims under 35 U.S.C. 101 for reciting or involving a law of nature, natural principle, natural phenomenon, or natural product, use revised form paragraph 7.05.13 (preceded by form paragraphs 7.04 and 7.05).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph text: 'the claimed invention is not directed to patent eligible subject matter. Based upon an analysis with respect to the claim as a whole, claim(s) [1] do not recite something significantly different than a judicial exception. The rationale for this determination is explained below: [2]'. Examiner Note: use this paragraph where claims have a law of nature/natural principle or natural phenomenon (e.g., a natural product) as a claim limitation.
